analysis.one_liner: Requires imported meat and poultry to be inspected by U.S. inspectors under the same standards as domestic products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Daschle and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in October 1990, but never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsors before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would amend the meat and poultry inspection laws so that meat and poultry coming into the country must meet the exact same inspection, sanitation, quality, species-verification, and chemical-residue standards applied to American-produced products [S2]. It would also require that those inspections be physically performed by U.S. government inspectors, rather than relying on foreign inspection systems [S2] [S3]. The idea was to close a gap where imported products could be certified under foreign inspection arrangements rather than checked by American personnel [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who would get an extra assurance that imported meat and poultry meet the same safety and quality standards as domestic products, and U.S. meat and poultry producers, who would no longer compete against imports certified under different, foreign-run inspection systems. Federal inspectors' role at the border would also be strengthened.

how_it_helps.text: Requires imported meat to be held to the 'same' inspection, sanitary, quality, species-verification, and residue standards applied to domestically produced meat, closing the wording gap in current law [S2] [S3].
Requires inspections of imported meat and poultry to be carried out by U.S. inspectors before entry, rather than being certified through foreign inspection systems [S2] [S3].
Extends the identical U.S.-inspector requirement to poultry imports under the Poultry Products Inspection Act [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Importers and foreign meat and poultry processors, who would face stricter, U.S.-performed inspection of their products, and to the extent compliance raises costs, grocery shoppers could see somewhat higher prices on imported meat and poultry.

drawbacks.text: Requiring U.S. inspectors to examine imports could significantly increase inspection costs and slow the flow of imported meat and poultry, costs that could be passed to consumers in higher grocery prices [S3].
The bill text contains no funding provision, so the added inspection workload would fall on federal agencies and ultimately taxpayers without a stated funding source [S3].

Opponents of equivalent-standard import inspection generally argue that foreign inspection systems approved by the U.S. already provide adequate protection; the bill would replace that system with direct U.S. personnel requirements [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit for consumers is real but modest: imports were already subject to U.S. inspection standards on paper; the bill's main change is insisting those inspections be performed by U.S. personnel and explicitly held to identical standards. The costs — more federal inspectors, slower imports, and possibly higher prices for imported meat — are real but unquantified in the record, and the bill offers no funding mechanism to cover them.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee from October 1990 until that Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on October 17, 1990 [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day; no further action was taken [S5] [S1].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and bills not passed by then die [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry importers and foreign processors are better off, because the stricter same-as-domestic U.S.-inspector requirement never took effect and the existing import certification system continued unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require U.S.-personnel inspection of meat and poultry imports under identical domestic standards.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 17, 1990 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Meat and poultry importers and foreign processors
against.what_they_did: Would have borne the cost of stricter, U.S.-performed inspection of imports; no direct lobbying activity appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry importers and foreign processors
industries.note: The bill would require their products to meet identical U.S. standards and be inspected by U.S. personnel, raising compliance costs and potentially slowing imports. Its death meant they kept the existing foreign-certification arrangements.
Domestic producers would face imports certified under the same standards and inspection regime, removing a competitive disadvantage from differing foreign inspection systems.

industries.industry: Federal meat and poultry inspection workforce
industries.note: The bill would expand the role of U.S. government inspectors in examining imported products before entry.
